displayQuote: With all this manure, there must be a pony somewhere!

meta.title: Who really said "With all this manure, there must be a pony somewhere!"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Reagan used this punchline on the record five times — but never in these words. Quote Investigator traces the gag to a banquet printed in 1902, a decade before Reagan was born.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'With all this manure, there must be a pony somewhere!'?
meta.ogDescription: Reagan really did love this joke. He just didn't write it — and in every full telling his punchline was "There's got to be a pony in here somewhere."

answer.label: Not Reagan’s line — an old joke he retold, in words he never used
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented telling: in print by January 1902 · made famous by Ronald Reagan, 1911–2004
answer.sourceLine: The pony gag is an anonymous American joke that Quote Investigator traces to 1902 in print ↗, reporting an Agate Club banquet held on December 20 — December 1901, since the issue carrying it is dated January 1902, a decade before Reagan was born. Reagan genuinely loved it and used the punchline on the record five times between 1981 and 1987, telling the full joke at least twice; in every full telling it ran “There’s got to be a pony in here somewhere” (once varied to “someplace”) — and in this joke he never once said “manure.”
answer.confidenceText: Reagan really did tell this joke — often. He just didn’t write it, and he didn’t say it this way.

source.heading: What Reagan actually said

docMeta.dd: Remarks and a Panel Discussion With Community Leaders on Welfare Reform
Public Papers of the Presidents: Ronald Reagan
“There’s got to be a pony in here somewhere.”

source.excerpt: You know, when I think of the welfare system, it reminds me of a story. And I know some here have heard me tell this before, and maybe everybody knows it, but pretend that you haven’t heard it because I like to tell this story. … [The psychiatrist fills one room with toys for the pessimist, and the other with “quite a quantity of what they clean out of the stable” for the optimist.] … And he was sitting there crying, and they said, “What are you crying about?” And he said, “Well, I know somebody’s going to come and take these away from me.” [Laughter] And they went down to the room with the optimist. And he was on top of that pile of stuff, and he was throwing it over his shoulder as fast as he could. And they said, “What are you doing?” He says, “There’s got to be a pony in here somewhere.” [Laughter]
trail: 1902 — the joke is already old. Quote Investigator’s earliest citation ↗ is the trade magazine Advertising Experience, dated January 1902, reporting a joke told by the Illinois state senator William E. Mason at the Agate Club banquet of December 20 — December 1901, on the arithmetic of a January issue: a boy finds frozen earth in his Christmas stocking and decides Santa “brought me a pony, but he must have got away.”

February 1953 — the punchline we know appears. QI documents the modern form in a newsletter of an Ohio group affiliated with Alcoholics Anonymous ↗: “With all this fertilizer, there’s got to be a pony somewhere.” Reagan was 41 and still acting.

1981–1987 — Reagan tells it, his way. The Public Papers index five Reagan uses of “pony in here.” In January 1982 remarks to the Executive Forum ↗ he delivers the punchline — “There’s got to be a pony in here somewhere” — then closes the speech with a bare callback: “There is a pony in here.”

1984 — the joke is already Reagan’s in print. Nineteen years before Robinson’s book, QI cites William Safire ↗ (“On Language: Punch-line English,” New York Times, 11 March 1984, p. A28) connecting the tale to Reagan — and treating “There must be a pony in here somewhere” as so familiar that the punchline alone would bring the whole joke to mind.

2003 — the wording is fixed in a book. Speechwriter Peter Robinson retells the joke in How Ronald Reagan Changed My Life, excerpted by CBS News ↗, as “With all this manure… there must be a pony in here somewhere!” That’s a staffer’s paraphrase, and the most-copied published form — but not the origin: QI documents “manure” versions circulating anonymously from 1949.
source.excerptNote: Bracketed text is our summary of the setup; everything in quotation marks is verbatim from the transcript. Note what’s missing: nowhere in this telling — or any other on the record — does Reagan say “manure,” and he never says “there must be a pony somewhere.”

sourceLink.text: Read the full 1987 remarks at the American Presidency Project

source.rightsNote: No located source contains this exact wording, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it. The pieces around it are clearer: the joke’s earliest documented forms (in print by 1902) are long in the public domain and anonymous; Reagan’s own tellings, quoted above, are US Government works in the Public Papers of the Presidents and are free of copyright. But the popular “With all this manure…” phrasing is closest to Peter Robinson’s How Ronald Reagan Changed My Life (2003), which is firmly in copyright — and even that reads “a pony in here somewhere.” We do not claim public domain for a wording we cannot tie to a specific work.

author.name: Ronald Reagan
author.heading: The man who made it famous
author.metaLine: 1911–2004 · 40th President of the United States · the joke's most famous teller
author.bio: Reagan was a professional storyteller long before he was a politician — a radio sportscaster, film actor, and corporate speaker who built a career on a well-timed anecdote. The pony joke was a signature: aide Ed Meese told speechwriter Peter Robinson, “If I heard him tell it once, I heard him tell it a thousand times.” But Reagan never claimed it as his own invention — in 1987 he introduced it by admitting “I know some here have heard me tell this before… but pretend that you haven’t heard it because I like to tell this story.”

On the joke’s pre-Reagan history, see “Quote Origin: There Must Be a Pony Somewhere,” Quote Investigator, December 13, 2013, which cites Advertising Experience (January 1902) as the earliest known printing. The popular “With all this manure…” wording matches no located transcript; its closest published form is Peter Robinson, How Ronald Reagan Changed My Life (New York: ReganBooks, 2003), though QI documents “manure” versions of the joke circulating anonymously from 1949 and William Safire connecting the tale to Reagan in the New York Times on March 11, 1984.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the popular version
misattribution.intro: This one fails on two independent counts — which is unusual. Most Reagan quote problems are “he never said it.” Here he said something very like it, hundreds of times, and it still isn’t his.

items.why: The gag predates him by a decade. Quote Investigator’s earliest citation ↗ is a January 1902 printing in Advertising Experience of a joke told at a banquet the previous December — Reagan was born in 1911. QI traces the joke through more than a century of retellings and identifies no single originator; it is anonymous folk humor.

Reagan’s documented punchline is “There’s got to be a pony in here somewhere” — not “there must be a pony somewhere.” And when telling this joke he conspicuously avoided the vulgar noun: in the 1987 welfare-reform remarks ↗ it is “quite a quantity of what they clean out of the stable.” The word “manure” appears in none of his tellings. (He could say it — he does, retelling a Truman anecdote in 1988 — he just never said it here.)

The familiar wording’s best-known published retelling — and the closest located match to it — is the one Reagan’s speechwriter set down in How Ronald Reagan Changed My Life (2003), excerpted by CBS News ↗: “With all this manure… there must be a pony in here somewhere!” Robinson was recounting a joke, not quoting a transcript. He didn’t coin it either: QI documents “manure” versions circulating anonymously from 1949, a “With all this fertilizer…” punchline in 1953, and William Safire pinning the tale to Reagan in the New York Times in 1984.

The pony line appears nowhere on Wikiquote’s Ronald Reagan page ↗ — not in the sourced quotes, not in Attributed, not in Misattributed. For a line this heavily pinned to him online, that silence is worth noting.

misattribution.truthLine: Reagan was the joke’s greatest performer, not its author — and the version in his mouth, preserved in the Public Papers ↗, was “There’s got to be a pony in here somewhere.”

context.heading: Why the pony stuck to Reagan
lead: Reagan didn’t just tell this joke — he governed with it. He reached for the pony when the economy was sour, when Congress was hostile, and when welfare reform stalled. It was a rhetorical move as much as a gag: a way of reframing bad news as buried opportunity without ever conceding the news was bad.

It worked so well that the punchline escaped the joke. In his January 1982 remarks to the Reagan Administration Executive Forum, delivered in the teeth of a recession, he told it in full — the two sons, the child psychiatrist, the friend with the racing stable — and then closed the speech on a bare callback: “There is a pony in here.” His staff picked the joke up as shorthand too. Ed Meese remembered that whenever something went wrong, somebody would be sure to say, “There must be a pony in here somewhere.” That’s how a hundred-year-old after-dinner joke became a Reagan quotation.
detailsBody: The confusion is understandable, and it isn’t really the public’s fault. Reagan told the joke in public, repeatedly, and told it well — but he told it as a piece of shared folk material, not as his own coinage. The joke was wearing his name in print long before any speechwriter wrote it down: William Safire was already pinning it to him in the New York Times in 1984. The polished “With all this manure…” version most people know matches no transcript, and its closest published form is the one speechwriter Peter Robinson set down in 2003 ↗, retelling from memory the joke his old boss loved — a book about Reagan, so the line sat on the page under Reagan’s name, in the form most often copied since.

The irony is that Reagan’s actual delivery is funnier and more characteristic than the tidy version now quoted in his name. He wouldn’t say the word. He worked around it — a friend with a racing stable, and “quite a quantity of what they clean out of the stable” — and let the audience do the last step themselves.
context.pull: The joke was older than Reagan. The optimism was the part that was his.
